passage:
Monday: Pema played football through the whole break in the blazing sun. Her water bottle stayed full in her bag. By maths her head throbbed, and when Samir borrowed her ruler she snapped, "Just take it!" and put her head on the desk. At home Mummy asked, "Did you drink anything today?" Pema thought hard. "Umm. No."
Wednesday: Pema made a rule: a sip at every whistle. Samir laughed, then copied her.
Friday: After a hard match, Pema noticed her mouth was dry and a small ache was starting behind her eyes. She drank before anyone reminded her. In maths she was cheerful, and she even lent Samir her ruler without being asked.

qa.q: What rule did Pema make on Wednesday?
qa.a: A sip at every whistle.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling in maths on Monday?
qa.a: She felt achy, tired and grumpy, which is why she snapped at Samir.

qa.q: What changed by Friday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Pema noticed her dry mouth and the starting ache and drank without a reminder, so she is learning to read her own body.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt when Pema snapped on Monday?
qa.a: Samir was probably surprised or a bit hurt, not knowing that Pema was thirsty and headachy.

grounding: Shows a child who forgets to drink while playing hard in the sun feeling headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

passage: Tarun, when your Dida was your age in Kolkata, I, Bidisha, played kho-kho in the school yard till my plaits were soaked. I never drank a drop; water was for babies, I thought. One April afternoon I came back to class with a pounding head and legs like wet rope. I shouted at my best friend Mitali for humming, then cried over a spelling test. Our games teacher, Mrs Ghosh, looked at my cracked lips and sat me under the neem tree with her own tin mug of water. "Your body was asking, and you weren't listening," she said. Next morning I carried a brass bottle to school, and I have carried one ever since.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Ghosh sit Bidisha?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was young Bidisha feeling back in class that afternoon?
qa.a: She felt achy, drained and irritable, so she shouted at Mitali and then cried over a spelling test.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bidisha's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mrs Ghosh noticing the cracked lips and giving her water; it taught Bidisha to listen to thirst, and she began carrying a bottle.

qa.q: How might Mitali have felt when Bidisha shouted about the humming?
qa.a: Mitali was probably hurt and puzzled, since the humming was harmless and the anger came from Bidisha's thirst.

grounding: Illustrates a child playing hard in the sun without drinking becoming headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

passage: Liam spent every minute of lunch chasing the ball across the dusty oval in Adelaide, shirt stuck to his back. He didn't stop at the drinking fountain; the game was too close. In maths his head began to throb. He snapped at Ines when she borrowed his ruler, then put his head down on his arms. "Did you drink anything at lunch?" Ines whispered. He thought. Nothing since breakfast. Mrs Park let him go to the fountain, and he drank for a long time. By the end of the lesson the throbbing had faded. That night he put his blue bottle next to his school shoes, and the next day he clipped it to the fence by the pitch.

qa.q: Where did Liam clip his bottle the next day?
qa.a: To the fence by the pitch.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling in maths?
qa.a: He felt headachy, tired and grumpy, enough to snap at Ines, without knowing thirst was the cause.

qa.q: What habit did Liam start, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Putting his bottle by his shoes and clipping it by the pitch, so he notices thirst and drinks even when the game is exciting.

qa.q: How might Ines have felt when Liam snapped about the ruler?
qa.a: Ines may have felt stung, but instead of snapping back she asked a caring question that helped.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild playing hard in the sun, forgetting to drink, feeling headachy and grumpy, and learning to carry a bottle.

passage: Parade practice for Republic Day ran all morning on the school ground, and Vishal marched in the front row, proud of his white shoes. His water bottle stayed in his bag in the classroom. By eleven his forehead ached and his legs felt heavy. He stamped the wrong foot twice, then muttered, "This is stupid," when Rekha Ma'am corrected him. She looked at his flushed face. "When did you last drink water?" He couldn't remember. She sent him to the shade with her own bottle and called a water break for the whole group. That afternoon Vishal wrote WATER on the back of his hand in pen. The next day his bottle came out to the ground with him.

qa.q: What did Vishal write on the back of his hand?
qa.a: WATER.

qa.q: Why did Vishal mutter "This is stupid"?
qa.a: He felt headachy, heavy and grumpy after marching in the sun without drinking, so a correction felt irritating.

qa.q: What did Rekha Ma'am do that helped more than scolding?
qa.a: She noticed his flushed face, asked about water, and gave the whole group a water break.

qa.q: How might Rekha Ma'am see Vishal's muttering?
qa.a: She reads it as a sign of thirst and heat rather than rudeness.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild exercising in the sun without drinking becoming achy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

passage:
Monday: Anand played gully cricket in the afternoon sun for three hours and came home with a headache, snapping at his brother Varun over the TV remote.
Wednesday: Same game, same headache. Mamma asked what he had drunk. "Nothing, I wasn't thirsty." But his lips were cracked, and he drained two glasses at once.
Saturday: Anand took a bottle to the lane and drank at every change of innings. Varun, keeping score, reminded him too. That evening he had no headache, and he let Varun choose the channel.

qa.q: When did Anand drink on Saturday?
qa.a: At every change of innings.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling on Monday evening?
qa.a: He felt headachy and grumpy, and took it out on Varun over the remote.

qa.q: What did Anand learn to notice?
qa.a: That not feeling thirsty doesn't mean he isn't; cracked lips and headaches are clues, so he drinks at set breaks.

qa.q: How might Varun see the change by Saturday?
qa.a: Varun gets a calmer brother who even lets him choose the channel, and joins in reminding him to drink.

grounding: Shows a child playing in the sun without drinking getting headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry water.

passage: Sunaina, don't leave your bottle on the table again. Let your grandfather Tenzin tell you why. When I was about your age, at the school in Kalimpong, I loved football more than food. One hot May day I played the whole lunch break, forgot my water, and by afternoon my head was pounding. I was so grumpy that I tore my friend Dawa's drawing when he laughed at me. The teacher sat me in the shade with a jug of water and asked, 'When did you drink today?' I couldn't remember. Slowly the headache faded, and I felt terrible about the drawing. From then on I tied my bottle to my bag strap and drank before every match.

qa.q: Where did young Tenzin tie the bottle?
qa.a: To the bag strap.

qa.q: How did young Tenzin feel in the afternoon after the match?
qa.a: He felt grumpy and sore-headed, so irritable that he tore Dawa's drawing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tenzin's story?
qa.a: The teacher sitting him in the shade with water and asking when he'd drunk; after that he carried his bottle and drank before matches.

qa.q: How might Dawa have felt when the drawing was torn?
qa.a: Dawa probably felt hurt and shocked, since he had only laughed.

grounding: A grandfather recalls forgetting water while playing in the sun as a schoolchild and learning to notice thirst.
